title: Helping Children Open Up About Their Feelings
intro: Big feelings can be hard to put into little words. A few small, everyday moments can help your child feel heard and understood.
sections: 1. Make room for every feeling
Let your child know that being sad, excited, worried, or angry is okay. Try saying, ‘I can see that was disappointing. I’m here with you.’ You don’t have to fix the feeling right away.
2. Give feelings a name
Use simple words during everyday moments: ‘You look proud of your tower!’ A feelings card can help when the right word is hard to find.
3. Share a little of your own
Model naming your feelings: ‘I felt frustrated when I couldn’t find my keys, so I took a slow breath.’ Keep your example short and reassuring.
4. Let play do the talking
Ask how a toy or story character might feel. Sometimes talking about Heartly’s day is easier than talking about their own.
5. Create a tiny check-in ritual
At bedtime or after school, ask, ‘What made your heart happy today? Was anything tricky?’ Listen without rushing. Connection matters more than the perfect answer.

title: Helping Children Through Frustration
intro: Learning to notice, name, and talk about feelings is a skill children can practise in small, playful ways.
sections: Start with noticing
A quick heartbeat, a big smile, or tight little fists can be clues to a feeling. Help your child notice these clues with curiosity and without judgment.
Build a feelings vocabulary
Begin with familiar words like happy, sad, and angry. As your child grows, explore words like disappointed, proud, and worried through stories and conversation.
Practise perspective-taking
Pause during a story and wonder together: ‘How might this character feel? What could a kind friend do?’ There doesn’t have to be only one answer.
Keep it playful
Use pictures, pretend play, and drawing to explore feelings. Follow your child’s interest and let them choose whether they want to talk.

title: Why Punishment Doesn't Build Cooperation
intro: You don’t need a perfect plan to make space for feelings. Try these simple activities with materials you already have at home.
sections: Draw your weather
Ask, ‘If your feelings were the weather today, what would they look like?’ Draw sunshine, clouds, rainbows, or a brand-new kind of weather together.
Play feelings charades
Take turns making a face or striking a pose. Guess the feeling together, then talk about when someone might feel that way.
Make a kindness jar
Write or draw little acts of kindness on scraps of paper. Pick one together: give a hug if someone wants one, share a toy, or say thank you.
Try a Heartly colouring break
Print a free activity, grab some crayons, and slow down together. Invite conversation without turning the activity into a quiz.
